segments.title: Opening and name check
segments.summary: The interview begins and Steinau gives his name.

segments.title: Why he never photographed Bourbon Street
segments.summary: Steinau explains he disliked Bourbon Street's music, felt uneasy there with a camera, and preferred listening to taking pictures.

segments.title: Celestin, Sharkey and George Lewis unphotographed; losing interest in Sharkey's band
segments.summary: He did not photograph Celestin, Sharkey or George Lewis on Bourbon Street. He first heard Sharkey's band in 1947 but lost interest once they played the same things nightly.

segments.chapter: Orrin Blackstone and the record shop
segments.title: Raymond Burke and Orrin Blackstone's Playback
segments.summary: Allen recalls Blackstone's praise of Raymond Burke; Steinau knew Blackstone only from a 1945 Esquire jazz book article and was too shy to approach him.

segments.chapter: Orrin Blackstone and the record shop
segments.title: Meeting Orrin, reading Down Beat and Esquire
segments.summary: Allen met Blackstone in 1945 and read Down Beat; Steinau read Esquire, which he feels slowed his interest in jazz.

segments.chapter: Orrin Blackstone and the record shop
segments.title: Blackstone's record shop, Parisian Room concerts and radio shows
segments.summary: Steinau learned of the shop in 1948 through a roommate and describes catching Roger Wolfe's jazz show and Parisian Room concerts; Allen describes the shop's layout.

segments.chapter: Orrin Blackstone and the record shop
segments.title: The shop's back room, Harvey's tune and auditioning bands
segments.summary: They recall a piano in the back room, Bourbon Street Bounce, and bands such as Emile Barnes's, Alvin Alcorn and Eddie Pearson auditioning.

segments.title: Auditions at Lenfant's restaurant and where it stood
segments.summary: They try to place Lenfant's restaurant on Airline Highway, where bands auditioned, and note which events each of them attended.

segments.title: Photographing Paul Barbarin's band and Emile Barnes's audition
segments.summary: Steinau photographed Paul Barbarin's band at the Yacht Club; Allen recalls Emile Barnes's audition at the shop before Christmas and the private-party circuit.

segments.title: How he found bands at parties; Celestin's second band
segments.summary: Friends took him to varied places, including a Stuart Bergen dance and a medical fraternity party where Celestin's second band played; Allen explains the second band's off-Bourbon jobs.

segments.title: Stumbling on a brass band parade near General Ogden Street
segments.summary: In 1951 Steinau heard a parade near his apartment; Allen talks about parades around town and how he learned of them.

segments.title: Birth and the family house on Broadway
segments.summary: Steinau was born in New Orleans in 1927 and lived in the same house at 2325 Broadway until age 24.

segments.title: Brass bands, high and low class music and Jim Crow
segments.summary: Steinau saw only Mardi Gras marching bands; they discuss class and racial divisions in the music of his youth and the lack of white brass bands.

segments.title: High school bands and Al Hirt
segments.summary: Steinau talks about strong white high school bands, Al Hirt as a product of that period, and the lack of jazz there.

segments.title: His mother's music, the Victrola and childhood songs
segments.summary: His mother played piano and taught him songs; he describes his wind-up Victrola, sheet music, vocal school and concerts.

segments.title: The Lizard on the Rail
segments.summary: Allen mentions the tune's original name; Steinau's mother sang a fragment and Johnny Wiggs played it.

segments.title: His father and Johnny Wiggs at school; Irvin Leclere and Triangle Jazz Blues
segments.summary: His father and Johnny Wiggs were schoolmates; Steinau also recounts learning in San Francisco that Irvin Leclere lived near his childhood home.

segments.title: Irvin Leclere's health and old age
segments.summary: Allen describes Leclere's pacemaker, his dancing and riding the bus around town.

segments.title: Johnny Wiggs as teacher and friend
segments.summary: They recall Wiggs's moods, his kindness, teaching, and his love of Bix and early jazz during walks on Rampart Street.

segments.title: Seeing Wiggs at the 1973 Jazz Club anniversary and his later death
segments.summary: Steinau saw Wiggs play on his honeymoon, where Wiggs mistook him for his father; he also recalls a radio announcer's memorial after Wiggs died.

segments.title: Finding the early jazz pioneers still alive
segments.summary: Steinau reflects on reading about jazz pioneers as if dead, then discovering many still playing in the late-1940s revival and treating them as patients.

segments.title: Age, the Bix legend and the romantic story of early death
segments.summary: They discuss musicians' ages and the myth of the short, meteoric jazz career.

segments.title: Radio listening in the 1930s and 1940s
segments.summary: Steinau recalls the swing and boogie-woogie he heard on radio before knowing what he liked.

segments.title: Big bands, the cabaret tax and playing for dancing
segments.summary: They discuss the lack of big bands in New Orleans, the cabaret tax ending dances, and George Lewis's band preferring to play for dancers.

segments.title: Discovering local white bands that played good jazz
segments.summary: Steinau was surprised to learn that bands from his high school dances played excellent jazz and says he was never a good dancer.

segments.title: Stuart Bergen's band, the flatbed truck and loud music
segments.summary: Allen remembers Stuart Bergen's band playing in Audubon Park on a truck; they talk about union concerts and liking loud music.
